question: When students change an answer on a multiple-choice exam, which kind of change is most common?
answer: Wrong to right. Kruger, Wirtz and Miller found about half of changes went from wrong to right and about a quarter from right to wrong, yet students believed sticking with a first instinct was safer. A right answer abandoned stings and is remembered; a lucky correction is quickly forgotten.
move: Count the times second thoughts saved you, not just the times they cost you.
ask: Which first instinct do I defend mainly because I remember the one time I ignored it and regretted it?
trap: Remembering the painful times a changed answer turned out to be wrong.
reference: Kruger, Wirtz & Miller, Counterfactual thinking and the first instinct fallacy, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2005
